html:
The Azusa Street Revival was a series of revival meetings in Los Angeles, led by the African American preacher William J. Seymour, that began in April 1906 and ran until about 1915. It launched Pentecostalism as a worldwide movement.

Seymour, the son of former slaves, had learned the teaching that believers should be "baptised in the Holy Spirit", with speaking in tongues as the sign. Barred from the church that had invited him, he held meetings in homes. On 9 April 1906 people began speaking in tongues, and the crowds grew so large that the meetings moved to an old church building at 312 Azusa Street.

The meetings ran almost daily, for hours, with loud prayer, singing, healing and tongues. What startled observers most was that Black and white, men and women, rich and poor worshipped together, and some leaders were women, at a time of hard racial segregation. Newspapers mocked it, but visitors came from across the country and abroad and carried the message home.

Within a few years missionaries from Azusa Street had taken Pentecostalism to Europe, Africa, India, China and Latin America. The movement soon split along racial lines in the United States, but it kept growing. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians now number in the hundreds of millions, with the fastest growth in Latin America, Africa and Asia. In countries such as Brazil and Guatemala they have changed both religion and politics, challenging the old dominance of the Catholic Church (see Latin America).
sum: The Azusa Street Revival was a series of revival meetings in Los Angeles, led by the African American preacher William J. Seymour, that began in April 1906 and ran until about 1915. It launched Pentecostalism as a worldwide movement.
